BLD-11.exclusive: Only people born of House Tessaran have the full working sixth finger. Outside the family a child is sometimes born with a small boneless nub, which midwives tie off;
BLD-11.story: The first Tessaran anyone wrote down with six fingers was Kallias, born in 603 at Tessar to a post-station keeper with ordinary hands. Midwives at the road stations called such hands a curse, and his mother kept them wrapped in cloth until he was five. He grew up in the stables of the Imperial Post. By 15 he was riding relays, and the station masters noticed that he could hold a hard-mouthed horse at the gallop with one hand while the other gripped the message case.
BLD-11.significance: In 1105 the hand is part of both claims to the Neck, the only land road between two continents. Each claimant must show it; a claimant without it would be mocked in both halves.

BLD-12.name: House Harrow
BLD-12.trait: Bull-blood: muscle mass 30–40% above normal from childhood
BLD-12.how: A broken copy of the gene that tells muscles when to stop growing. With one broken copy a Harrow is only strong; with two the brake is off entirely, and muscle keeps building from infancy to 30–40% more than other men carry.
BLD-12.inherit: Recessive in full form. Carriers with one copy are merely strong; about 1 in 4 children of two carriers is a full bull. The house marries Harrowsett cousins to breed bulls.
BLD-12.cost: Enormous appetite, poor stamina in long marches, stiff joints by 40 and weak hearts: few full bulls live past 50. Their heavy frames need big horses, and they tire quickly in a long fight.
BLD-12.exclusive: The broken copy came from Oswy Harrow alone, and every carrier since descends from him. Full bulls are born only when two Harrow carriers marry, so the house weds its Copperham heirs to Harrowsett…
BLD-12.ancestor: Lord Gunnar Harrow the Bull, who threw an orc war-chief from his horse bare-handed
BLD-12.story: The broken copy came into the house with its founder, Oswy Harrow, born in 925, a captain of the Crown Wall road who was said to be as strong as two men and who could lift a laden cart wheel off the ground. He was a carrier, not a bull, and so were half his children. For three generations the Harrows of Harrowsett were known only as a strong family that ate well. Then in 1000 Wulfstan Harrow married his cousin Elfgiva of Harrowsett, both carriers, because the march had few families of rank. Their son Gunnar, born in 1001, had the arms of a grown man at six and ate as much as three farmhands.
BLD-12.significance: The bull-blood explains why the man commanding Aldmark's 8,000 soldiers on the Gordush wants a war now. Garrick Harrow is a full bull with perhaps two years of heart left, and he means to cross the river the day after May Fair, seize Tarn Halfblood and win back the upper Gordush before he dies.

BLD-13.name: House Ravenscar
BLD-13.trait: Owl-eyes: sees by starlight almost as well as others by dusk
BLD-13.how: The back of the eye holds far more rod cells, the cells that see in dim light, and fewer cone cells for color and sharp daylight sight. Starlight is enough to see a rider at 200 m, but noon sun floods the eye.
BLD-13.inherit: Dominant: one copy is enough, and about half the children of a carrier have it.
BLD-13.cost: Dazzled and half-blind in bright sun, with migraines at noon; poor color sight, so they cannot read banner colors by day. They veil their eyes with dark gauze in daylight and fight best at night.
BLD-13.exclusive: Every carrier descends from Hereward. The house rule is that a Ravenscar of the blood marries someone who takes the Ravenscar name and raises the children at Northmoor, as Sir Wystan Holloway did in…
BLD-13.ancestor: Lady Maud Ravenscar the Owl, the night raider
BLD-13.story: The owl-eyes appeared in Hereward, born about 890, a forester's son of the Northmoor chase on the Oak Line, below the burned hill called Raven Scar. As a boy he squinted and wept in summer noon and saw nothing of the colors of the Kingsmere banners, but at night he could walk the chase without a lantern and find a poacher's snare by starlight. The last Fairrush kings made him their verderer, the keeper of the royal chase, because no poacher could hide from him after dark. His children had the same eyes, or did not, about half and half.
BLD-13.significance: The owl-eyes are why Aldmark can scout and raid across the Gordush at night when the orcs sleep, and why the empire's spymistress sits on the Imperial Council. Corbin Ravenscar plans to map Tarn Halfblood's camp at Graknak on the moonless nights of early 1105.

BLD-14.name: House Montaro
BLD-14.trait: Bleeds laughing: feels little pain or fear and heals wounds about a third faster
BLD-14.how: A change near the gene that breaks down the body's own pain-dulling and calming substances (like the rare change found in a few Earth families with the same gifts) leaves those substances high in the blood all the time.
BLD-14.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of a carrier have it.
BLD-14.cost: Burns, broken bones and deep wounds go unnoticed until they fester; many die of wounds they ignored or of reckless charges. Carriers are often forgetful, and their calm reads to others as coldness.
BLD-14.exclusive: The Vitia fostering. Every child of Montaro blood is given the nettle test at five, and any child with the laughing blood is raised at Vitia under the Montaro name: children of Montaro men born out…
BLD-14.ancestor: General Cesare Montaro, Who Bled Laughing
BLD-14.story: The first carrier was Ruggero Montaro, born at the citadel of Vitia in 927, grandson of the castellan Taddeo Montaro. His mother first noticed it when he was three and put his hand into the hearth to fetch a roasting chestnut, then laughed at the blister. He never cried when he fell, and he walked on a thorn in his heel for a week until it festered. In the winter of 952, as a young sergeant, he held the wall of the Montessa Gate all night against Crown foothill bandits who had come for the gate's grain. In the morning the castle surgeon found that his shin was broken;
BLD-14.significance: In 1105 the laughing blood commands Varenna's army. Dario Montaro is Lord Marshal of 78,000 men and leader of the War Party, Vittor holds the Crown Road army of 9,000 at Ardata, and Ottavia leads the Laughing Company.

BLD-15.name: House Cinderwell
BLD-15.trait: Oak tendons: tendons and ligaments far thicker than normal, almost never torn
BLD-15.how: A change in the gene for the main building fiber of tendons and ligaments makes them grow thicker and stiffer than other people's. A Cinderwell's knees, shoulders and ankles take loads that tear other men's sinews, but the joints bend less.
BLD-15.inherit: Dominant: one copy is enough, and about half the children of a carrier have it.
BLD-15.cost: Stiff joints: poor flexibility, slow to turn, poor at climbing and swimming. Carriers tire their knees and backs in old age and cannot chase a fleeing enemy.
BLD-15.exclusive: Every carrier descends from Tobin. The house marries into yeoman families of the guard, and all children of the blood are raised at Kingsdale and trained in the Shield Yard, where the tendons are…
BLD-15.ancestor: Sir Tobin Cinderwell, who held the gate of Ashmere with a shield for a day
BLD-15.story: The oak tendons began with Tobin Cinderwell, born 940 on the family's ash farm near Kingsdale. No Cinderwell before him had them. He was a stiff child who could not touch his toes or climb the orchard trees, and the other boys mocked him for it. But at 14 he carried a plough-ox yoke on his shoulders across a field, and at the May Fair wrestling no one could twist his knee or wrench his shoulder, though they threw him often enough because he turned slowly. A Temple physician who saw him at Ashmere wrote that the boy's heel cords were as thick as a man's thumb.
BLD-15.significance: The Cinderwells stand closer to Ashmere's crown than anyone. Sir Owain Cinderwell witnessed the hidden clause and swore silence, and he means to make the king tell Rowena before Return Day or tell her himself. His sister Bryony guards Rowena's door.

BLD-16.name: House Zahiri
BLD-16.trait: Thirstless: goes two days in desert heat on half the water others need
BLD-16.how: A changed gene keeps the kidney's water-saving signal always on, so the kidneys pull back far more water and make urine two to three times more concentrated than normal. The same concentrated urine lets salts crystallize, which is why nearly every carrier grows kidney stones.
BLD-16.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of one carrier have it. The house marries cousins, so some children get it from both parents; they pass stones in boyhood and rarely live past 40.
BLD-16.cost: Kidney stones in almost every adult carrier, often from the twenties; many die of kidney failure or a blocked stone in their fifties. The Dry Month fast makes the stones worse. Children with the blood from both parents pass stones in boyhood and rarely live past 40.
BLD-16.exclusive: Only descendants of Zahir I carry it. By the house law of 815 Zahiri daughters marry Zahiri cousins or men who take the Zahiri name and live in the Yasesh household, so every child of a carrier…
BLD-16.ancestor: Sultan Zahir the Thirstless, who crossed the Burning Waste
BLD-16.story: The trait began with Zahir himself, born in 760 to Nadim Idrisi and a merchant's daughter of Marira; neither parent, nor any Idrisi before him, had it. As a boy he drank little and passed little water, and his nurses thought him sickly. In exile at Tamar he rode with the natron caravans to the edge of the Burning Waste and found that he could ride a whole day on half a water-skin while the Tamari drivers staggered. At 19 he passed his first stone and screamed through a night the Tamari court still talked about. He built his return on the gift.
BLD-16.significance: In 1105 a war hangs on a sickbed. Grand Admiral Jalal cannot sail on Sabra without the Sultan's own voice, and the Sultan's voice depends on his kidneys. If Zahir IV dies this spring, the Divan must choose between a regent heir who hides the same sickness and an admiral who wants war.

BLD-17.name: Clan Bahar
BLD-17.trait: Sand-eyes: sharp distance sight that is not dazzled by desert glare
BLD-17.how: A dense layer of yellow pigment in the center of the eye soaks up glare and blue light, so the eye sees far and sharp in noon sun. The same eyes have fewer working cells for dim light, so carriers see poorly at dusk and are nearly blind on a moonless night.
BLD-17.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of one carrier have it.
BLD-17.cost: Poor sight at dusk and near-blindness on moonless nights. A clan of guides whose chief's line cannot read the stars on a dark night must rely on others' eyes, and raiders strike them in the dark.
BLD-17.exclusive: Only descendants of Rashid Bahar carry it, and they are all of the Bahar chief's line. The roughly 110,000 common Bahar herders do not have it.
BLD-17.ancestor: Rashid Bahar the Far-Seer, clan chief
BLD-17.story: The first carrier was Rashid Bahar, born in 960 to a younger son of the Bahar chief; no Bahar before him had it. As a small boy he stared at the noon dunes without squinting and could name a rider's clan by his camel at 5 km, while other children wept from the glare. The same boy fell over tent ropes at dusk and got lost between tents on dark nights, and his mother tied a bell to his wrist. The clan thought him half-blind.
BLD-17.significance: The sand-eyes are part of why one family has held the Speakership of the largest land on the map for 104 years: the Noon Lances are the confederation's best cavalry, and the council half believes the Bahar see farther. In 1105 that belief is fraying.

BLD-18.name: House Tamaren
BLD-18.trait: Fever-proof: rarely catches the delta fevers that kill others
BLD-18.how: One changed copy of a blood gene makes the red cells a poor home for the marsh fever, so carriers rarely sicken or die of it (like Earth's sickle-cell trait).
BLD-18.inherit: Carriers have one copy and are protected; about half the children of one carrier carry it. When two carriers have children, about 1 in 4 gets two copies and the blood sickness.
BLD-18.cost: Children of two carriers have about a 1 in 4 chance of the blood sickness and rarely live past 20; the royal habit of cousin marriage makes it common. The blood gives no protection against flux, plague or famine.
BLD-18.exclusive: Only descendants of Nefira carry it, and since 966 only descendants of Queen Neferu. The law of 989 means a king's heir must have a Tamaren mother, and Tamaren daughters marry Tamaren cousins, so no…
BLD-18.ancestor: Queen Nefira of the Delta, first of the dynasty
BLD-18.story: The trait began with Nefira, born in 612 to the Sethepi lord of Marira; her parents did not have it, and the delta fevers killed two of her brothers before they were ten. Nefira waded the reed beds with the fowlers, slept in the papyrus marshes on hunting trips, and in years when half the delta shook with fever she caught it once, lightly. The delta people said the Mother loved her. Her father, who had lost two sons, kept her in the delta rather than send her to the healthier upper valley, and her nurses swore she was the Mother's own child. She learned to use it.
BLD-18.significance: In 1105 the blood is part of the king's claim to be the Mother's son, and it is the one proof that Nefira's line survives in the king whatever the Talim jar says about Amenhar I. It is also the house's danger.

BLD-19.name: House Kanemba (the Runner's blood)
BLD-19.trait: Runner's blood: can run 100 km in a day and keep going
BLD-19.how: A change in the gene for the receptor that tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, the kind found in rare Earth families of endurance athletes. The marrow over-answers the body's signal, so carriers have about a fifth more red cells than other people.
BLD-19.inherit: Dominant: a carrier passes it to about half of his or her children, sons and daughters alike. Children who get it from both parents, common in the imperial line because of the Senior Wife Rule, have the thickest blood and the earliest strokes.
BLD-19.cost: Thick blood. Carriers suffer headaches, red faces in the heat and nosebleeds in the highlands, and many die suddenly of strokes or clots between 40 and 60; five emperors died of strokes between 44 and 49. Children with the blood from both parents are the worst hit.
BLD-19.exclusive: Only people sung into the Kanemba line carry it. The Law of the Sung Line (931) requires the High Rememberer to sing every child of an emperor, prince or Runner-kin man or woman into the Kanemba line…
BLD-19.story: The Kanemba of Anumba carried messages for the Tedana kings from at least the 820s, and runners' families noticed stamina the way herders notice a good bull. The gift was first written into the Rememberers' songs with Dembe Kanemba. On 3 March 851 an Omamba war band crossed toward Anumba, and King Ajani at Zanara needed the Anumba spearmen at the Lotapa crossing before the raiders. Dembe ran the 206 km in two days and a night, drank at every post, and reached Anumba still able to speak the order clearly. The spearmen held the crossing and the raid failed.
BLD-19.significance: The blood decides who rules Zanara and for how long. Every emperor since Mosi the Runner has been sung into the Kanemba line, and every one who carried the blood except the founder died of a stroke before 50.

BLD-20.name: House Asfari (the Twin-born)
BLD-20.trait: Twin-born: women of the line bear twins in about 1 birth in 3
BLD-20.how: A variant of a gene that sets the level of the pituitary hormone that ripens eggs (FSH). Women who carry it often ripen two eggs in one cycle, so they conceive non-identical twins in about one birth in three. Men carry and pass the variant but it does nothing to them.
BLD-20.inherit: Dominant but shown only in women: a carrier, man or woman, passes it to about half of his or her children, and only daughters show it. So twins come through the mothers of the line, and a king's twins depend on his queen being of the blood.
BLD-20.cost: Twin births kill mothers: five of nine royal Asfari mothers since 1029 died in or soon after childbirth, and many twins are born early and small. Each generation brings two heirs of one age, and the twin-born law splits the realm between them.
BLD-20.exclusive: The Cord Law of 1022 keeps it inside the house. Asfari daughters marry only Asfari men or the lords of the three cord houses.
BLD-20.ancestor: The Twin Kings Asfar and Asmar of Abara
BLD-20.story: The first carrier the Rememberers can name is Lady Tsehay of Nusalo, born in 902, a daughter of the lords of Nusalo who married her cousin, the heir of the house, in 919. She bore twins in 921, again in 925 and a third pair in 932, and lived through all three births, which the Nusalo songs count as her real wonder. Highland custom holds that village twins share one soul and gives the younger to the Rememberers, but the lords of Nusalo were rich enough to pay a soul-price of 100 cattle for each pair and keep both children. Tsehay's daughters bore twins too, and so did their daughters.
BLD-20.significance: The blood is Abara's law of succession. Under the Compact only twin-born heirs may share the crown, and royal twins come only from the cord. In 1105 neither king has a twin son: Yared has one daughter and Yonas is a widower.

BLD-21.name: House Keshari (the Boneless)
BLD-21.trait: Boneless: joints that bend far beyond normal; can slip bonds and squeeze through small gaps
BLD-21.how: A change in a gene for one of the collagens, the proteins that make ligaments, joint capsules and skin tough. Carriers' ligaments stretch far more than other people's, so their fingers and elbows bend backward and their shoulders and thumbs can be slipped out of joint and back again.
BLD-21.inherit: Dominant: a carrier passes it to about half of his or her children, sons and daughters alike.
BLD-21.cost: Joints dislocate easily, skin tears and heals slowly, and arthritis comes early: Kombo fell when a knee gave way, Nuru died when his shoulder failed on the Pepper Hall roof, and Faraji's knees are failing at 32.
BLD-21.exclusive: The Keshari claim every child of their blood. A child of a Keshari father or mother is named Keshari, taught at the Rope Hall and bound to the house by a pepper-weight contract, and Keshari…
BLD-21.ancestor: Nuru Keshari the Boneless, acrobat-thief who became Prince of Kesh
BLD-21.story: The family remembers Sauti Keshari, born 945, a rigger's wife of the Kesh harbor lanes who could fold her thumb flat against her wrist and did it at fairs for coppers. Her son Pili, born 968, was the first to turn the trick into a living. At the Harvest Home of 985, at 17, he won the climb up the Pepper Hall roof by wedging his hands and feet into gaps between the roof timbers that no other climber could use. That winter the harbor guards caught him in a pepper store and locked him in the iron stocks on the quay; in the morning the stocks were empty and still locked.
BLD-21.significance: The blood is the reason House Keshari rules the League at all. The council elected Nuru for a theft only his joints made possible, and the harbor lanes still treat the Keshari as climbers who became princes.

BLD-22.name: House Sevrin
BLD-22.trait: Bear-blood: men grow to 195–215 cm and very broad
BLD-22.how: A changed gene fails to hold back the small growth gland under the brain. In about one carrier son in three the gland swells in boyhood and pours out growth hormone, so the boy grows to 195–215 cm with heavy jaw, hands and feet.
BLD-22.inherit: About half the children of a carrier inherit the gene, men and women alike, but it shows only in about one carrier son in three and almost never in daughters; the others carry it unseen and can pass it on.
BLD-22.cost: Heart failure, joint pain, headaches and moments of blindness; the tallest Sevrins rarely live past 45, and the doorpost custom sends healthy short princes to monasteries.
BLD-22.exclusive: Only Sevrins carry it. The house keeps a roll of every measuring at the doorpost and of every Sevrin child, and sons of Sevrin daughters married abroad are watched;
BLD-22.ancestor: King Radoslav Sevrin the Bear, 211 cm
BLD-22.story: The first Sevrin giant on record is Borislav, born at Sevina in 700 to an Eastfolk officer of the Solen legions. His father was of middle height. Borislav was an ordinary boy until 12, when he began to grow a hand's breadth a year, and by 18 he stood a head over other men. The legion of the Eastern March made him its standard-bearer, because men could see the black bear standard over his head from anywhere on a field. He learned early that men follow what they can see. His headaches began at 25, and he hid them.
BLD-22.significance: In 1105 the bear-blood decides the timetable of the north-east. Stanislav, 33, has the headaches and blind moments that killed the giants before him, and he is pushing the staged rising and the Neck war to finish what he can before he dies.

BLD-23.name: House Dravic
BLD-23.trait: The Listener's ears: hears whispers through a door and footsteps at 200 m
BLD-23.how: A changed gene leaves the bone over one of the inner ear's balance canals paper-thin or open. Sound then reaches the inner ear through the skull as well as through the air, so a Dravic hears whispers through a wall, footsteps at 200 m and even her own heartbeat.
BLD-23.inherit: Dominant: about half of the children of a carrier have it, sons and daughters alike. Every carrier alive descends from Queen Ludmila, in whom it first appeared.
BLD-23.cost: Loud noise is painful; drums and horns bring dizziness and collapse; ringing in the ears grows with age until many are half deaf; a carrier cannot lead an army that marches to drums, and the Tusk Clans know it.
BLD-23.exclusive: Every carrier descends from Queen Ludmila, the first to have it; the only living carriers are Queen Milena and Princess Ludmila.
BLD-23.ancestor: Queen Ludmila Dravic the Listener, who heard assassins through a wall
BLD-23.story: Ludmila Dravic was born at Drevna in 984, the only one of King Ozren's five children to live, and neither her father nor her mother had unusual ears. As a baby she screamed at the bells of the island monasteries across the lake. At six she could name which servant was walking the corridor by the sound of the step, and at ten she told her father which of his lords had been arguing in the next room through a stone wall. Her nurses thought her touched and a priest was brought to bless her. King Ozren saw a use instead.
BLD-23.significance: In 1105 the Listener's ears decide who will rule Drevna. The Lake Council may set aside an heir who cannot lead the army, and the princess collapses at drums, while the clause that allows it was slipped into the Code in 1066 and the older copy survives.

BLD-25.name: House Ranavir
BLD-25.trait: Unpoisoned: resists arsenic, the poisoner's favorite
BLD-25.how: A stronger form of the liver enzyme that tags arsenic for the kidneys: carriers turn arsenic into a harmless form and pass it in their water within a day, so small doses never build up and they survive about four times the dose that kills others.
BLD-25.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of one carrier carry it. When two carriers marry, about one child in four gets a double dose and is stillborn, one in four is free of it, and half carry it.
BLD-25.cost: Stillbirths: two carriers lose about one child in four in the womb, and cousin marriage makes that common, so the house is always short of heirs. The yearly test is itself a danger: a child who does not carry the blood sickens and can die if the dose is misjudged.
BLD-25.exclusive: Only people born to a Ranavir carrier can carry it, and the yearly arsenic test shows exactly who does. Sons who carry it stay in the house;
BLD-25.ancestor: Raja Vikram Ranavir the Unpoisoned, who survived seven poisonings
BLD-25.story: The trait began in the hill lords of Devesh, whose town sits on rock full of yellow stone, the arsenic ore of the Monsoon Coast. Nobody knows which Ranavir first carried it; the family's chant names Bhim Ranavir (846-912), lord of Devesh, as "the first to drink and stand". In the drought of 889 the town's shallow wells dried, and Bhim's household drew water for a whole dry season from a deep well cut through the yellow rock. By the rains his servants and soldiers from the delta had dark spots on their skin, horny palms and numb, burning feet, and nine of them died.
BLD-25.significance: In 1105 the Ranavir blood decides who rules seven million people. If Prince Vikram's failed test comes out, or if he dies of his monsoon fevers, the temples choose among the Ranavir men, and Lord Kiran, who carries the blood and has two sons who passed the test, is buying their favor with 30,000…

BLD-26.name: House Maruang
BLD-26.trait: Storm-sense: feels falling air pressure in the ears and sinuses a day before a cyclone
BLD-26.how: A family shape of the skull: unusually large air cells in the bone behind the ear and in the cheek sinuses, narrow tubes that let air out of the middle ear only slowly, and a lining crowded with pressure-sensing nerves.
BLD-26.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of one carrier have it, sons and daughters alike. It shows by the age of five or six, when a child cries and holds its head before storms. The trait was formerly recorded as a fever-proof blood enzyme passed through mothers;
BLD-26.cost: Weeks of pressure headaches through every cyclone season, when a carrier is often too sick to rule or fight; frequent ear infections, and deafness in one ear by 50 for many.
BLD-26.exclusive: Only children of a carrier have it. Since 895 the Law of the Closed Harbor has let a Maruang daughter marry only a Maruang cousin or a man who takes the Maruang name and lives in the palace, so every…
BLD-26.ancestor: Bima Maruang the Stormwise, first known carrier (the Great Cyclone of 858)
BLD-26.story: The first Maruang known to have it was Bima Maruang (821-879), a harbor chief's son of Amberport. As a boy he cried and held his head before storms, and his father beat him for weakness. As a man he learned that the ache came a night and a day before the wind, and that it came hardest before a cyclone. In September 858, when every fleet of the isles was loading spice for the run to Kesh, the ache came. Bima kept every Amberport boat in harbor and his captains called him a coward. The next day the Great Cyclone struck.
BLD-26.significance: In 1105 the storm-sense is part of the balance of the Eastern Gulf. The Amber fleet sails to take the Isle of Pearls in April and may still be at sea when the cyclones begin in August; a Maruang aboard is worth a dozen galleys.

BLD-27.name: House Kharsan (the lean-blood)
BLD-27.trait: Lean-blood: survives famine on half rations for months
BLD-27.how: A change in one gene that governs fat storage makes the body turn food into fat quickly and, when food runs short, lower its burning rate and live on that fat while sparing muscle, like the thrifty-gene variants of some island and desert peoples on Earth.
BLD-27.inherit: Dominant: one copy is enough. About half the children of a carrier have it, sons and daughters alike.
BLD-27.cost: In good years they grow fat and suffer sugar sickness: thirst, sores on the feet that do not heal, blindness and lost limbs between 45 and 60. Few khans of the line have died old and whole.
BLD-27.exclusive: It runs only in House Kharsan. The Tent Law of 926 keeps it there: a Kharsan daughter's husband must come to live at Kharsa and their children are raised Kharsan, so every carrier belongs to a branch…
BLD-27.story: The first Kharsan the songs remember is Kharsa the Thin, a herder of the Blue Wind born about 765. In the killing winter of 788, when a thaw and a hard frost sealed the grass under ice, his family's herd died down to the last 40 sheep. Kharsa drove them alone for three months through the snow on a strip of dried meat a day and brought 31 of them to spring grass at Torkul. His two brothers, bigger men, died of hunger on the same road. The herders noticed that Kharsa had grown thin but never weak.
BLD-27.significance: The lean-blood is why the Kharsan rule and why they may stop. It made Ulagan khan and made the Wind Empire, whose yams, Saddle Law and grudges still shape the steppe. In 1105 it is the hidden center of the Nine Winds' crisis.

BLD-28.name: House Sabrani
BLD-28.trait: Salt-skin: sweats freely and stays cool in heat that fells others
BLD-28.how: Carriers have far more working sweat glands than other people and start sweating sooner, so their bodies shed heat fast. Their sweat also carries more salt than normal, so they lose salt and water quickly and cramp and collapse when either runs short.
BLD-28.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of one carrier have it, sons and daughters alike.
BLD-28.cost: Carriers lose salt and water fast. Without both they cramp and collapse sooner than anyone, and a long fast can kill them; two children died in the Dry Month before 1035, and Emir Nasir died after the fast of 1086.
BLD-28.exclusive: Only descendants of Bakr Sabrani carry it. Farid's house law of 1035 makes every child of a Sabrani parent, son or daughter, a Sabrani by name and household, and husbands of Sabrani daughters live in…
BLD-28.story: The first carrier was Bakr Sabrani, born in 935 into a family of pearl merchants at Sabra; neither his parents nor his brothers had it. As a boy he sweated through his shirt even in winter, craved salt so badly that he licked it from the fish-drying racks, and cramped on the pearling boats when others did not. When he was 15 he collapsed on a boat in the Dry Month and nearly died, and his mother learned to give him salted water at dusk. The family thought it a weakness.
BLD-28.significance: In 1105 Sabra's defense depends on the blood. Its doctrine is to hold the Sabun road with camel riders and fight at midday, where Sabrani officers outlast any enemy, and Nuri Hazimi's Camel School trains for that.

BLD-29.name: The Brine line
BLD-29.trait: Sea-steady: never seasick; perfect balance on a pitching deck
BLD-29.how: A variant in the balance organs of the inner ear lets them settle quickly to any steady rocking and trust the eyes over the ear's own sense of motion, so a carrier never feels the clash of signals that causes seasickness and keeps his footing on a rolling deck.
BLD-29.inherit: Dominant: about half of a carrier's children have it. It shows the first time a child is taken out in a rough sea, usually by age six.
BLD-29.cost: On land the ground sways for days after every voyage; with age the dizziness lasts between voyages. Carriers fall on stairs and quays, and they feel no warning of bad weather in their bodies, so they take risks at sea that others refuse.
BLD-29.exclusive: The trait began with Tamsin of Brinehole in 998, so only her descendants carry it. Under the Articles, children of crew are crew, and every child of a Brine is entered in the share-book at the Shrine…
BLD-29.story: The first known carrier was Tamsin of Brinehole, born in 998 in a salt-boat hamlet on the south shore of Blackreef Isle. Her parents were salters who were as sick as anyone on rough water. Tamsin was not. As a girl she rowed the salt boats out to the Gull Isle pans in winter seas that kept the men ashore, and she could stand on the gunwale of a boat in a swell while her brothers lay retching in the bilge. The hamlet thought it was luck from the Drowned Queen.
BLD-29.significance: The Brine balance is part of how Blackreef survives. It won the Brotherhood its winter sailing, which broke the blockade of 1054–1055, and its dragon, which needs steady hands on burning rafts at night. In 1105 it is also the Brotherhood's weak point.

BLD-30.name: Line of Gorath
BLD-30.trait: Blood fury: in a fight, huge surges of fight hormones; no fear, faster reactions and harder blows for three to five minutes
BLD-30.how: Carriers have larger adrenal glands that fire far more easily than other orcs'. In a fight they flood the blood with adrenaline: the heart races, pain and fear fade and the fast muscle fibers fire at their limit for three to five minutes.
BLD-30.inherit: Dominant: one copy is enough, and about half the children of a carrier have it, sons and daughters alike. It first shows in a fight, usually between 12 and 16.
BLD-30.cost: Hearts and brains fail young: heart attacks and strokes in the 30s and 40s. After a fury carriers faint, their lips turn grey and they cannot stop once it starts, so they sometimes strike friends. Few live past 50.
BLD-30.exclusive: Every carrier descends from Gorath, because the trait began in him; there is no fury in any other orc line.
BLD-30.ancestor: Gorath the Great, uniter of the Horde
BLD-30.story: The blood fury began with Gorath himself. His mother, Mother Hagra of the Urgol clan, and his father, the Vrakoth-born rider Durr One-Ear, were steady people, and the Grey Mothers' hides show no fury in either kin. Gorath was a big, quiet boy until August 1012, when the Urgol clan fought a Goroth kin over the wells of the Krugak and Durr was killed. Gorath, 14, rode into the fight without armor, killed three grown riders and kept striking at a fourth who had already surrendered, until his cousins dragged him off.
BLD-30.significance: The war-chief of 1.6 million people carries a heart that has already failed him twice, on the eve of a possible war with Aldmark. If Vrag dies in a fury charge in the spring of 1105, the Horde must choose a new war-chief in the middle of a war, and the Line of Gorath has only a wrestler and a…

BLD-31.name: Clan Ironhide
BLD-31.trait: Thick hide: skin about twice as thick as other orcs', so cuts are shallow
BLD-31.how: The deep layer of the skin grows about twice as thick and dense with tough fibers, so blades, claws and horns that would open an orc's flesh barely break through. The thick skin has fewer and smaller sweat glands and holds in heat, so carriers overheat even faster than other orcs.
BLD-31.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of a carrier have it, from either parent. It can be felt in a baby's skin within a month of birth.
BLD-31.cost: They sweat poorly and overheat faster than other orcs, who already overheat. Two clan-mothers of the line have died of heat at summer gatherings, and carriers cannot fight long in summer. The hide does not stop crossbow bolts or spear points.
BLD-31.exclusive: Every carrier descends from Uzma, in whom the change began. Grakka sent mostly non-carriers out in marriage.
BLD-31.ancestor: Grakka Ironhide, war-mother of the Tusk Clans
BLD-31.story: The first carrier was Uzma, born in 971 in the Grakmar clan, which grazed the grass around the winter camp at Grakmar. Neither her mother nor her father had the hide; the clan's hides show nothing like it before her. As a child she never cut her feet on the stony ground, and her mother's knife slipped when it should have pierced a boil. In January 988, at 17, she was caught in a knife fight over a stolen mare at the winter camp. She took three cuts to the arm and side that barely passed her skin, and killed both her attackers. The clan called her Ironhide.
BLD-31.significance: The War-Mother who rules 700,000 people and holds the silk tolls, and her only heir, both carry a skin that may kill them in summer. A war with Drevna over the withheld rye would come in the spring of 1105 and could run into the heat.

BLD-32.name: The Grey Mothers
BLD-32.trait: Long life: women of the line live to 80–90 against 45–60 for most orcs; the men of the line to about 65–70
BLD-32.how: A change in the tiny energy-making bodies inside every cell, which a child gets only from its mother's egg. These burn more cleanly and wear the body less, so it ages more slowly: grey hair at 45 instead of 30, strength kept into the 70s.
BLD-32.inherit: Through mothers only. Every child of a woman of the line carries it. Sons carry it and live longer than other orcs, but cannot pass it on. It is strongest in daughters.
BLD-32.cost: Few children: two or three in a lifetime, borne late, so the line never grows and could die out in one generation of sons. Grey Mothers outlive their children and grandchildren, and their long memories make them feared and hated.
BLD-32.exclusive: The trait passes only from mother to child, so only children of women of the line carry it, and a man of the line cannot pass it on.
BLD-32.ancestor: Old Mother Shagra, who lived to 91
BLD-32.story: The first Grey Mother was Mother Hesh, born about 590 among the eastern clans that grazed around Goroth and the northern shore of the Salt Sea. Her own mother died at 41, as orc women do, and nothing in her mother's kin was unusual. Hesh was. She did not go grey at 30. She bore her first child at 27 and her last at 49. She outlived four husbands and all her sisters and still rode to the Great Ride at 80. Her three daughters aged as slowly; her son lived to 68, but his children were ordinary. The clans used her memory before they understood her blood.
BLD-32.significance: The Grey Mothers decide who leads 1.6 million people. At the Great Ride of 21 June 1105 they mean to name an heir to Vrag before his heart fails, and Mother Ugra has chosen Tarn over Skarn Redhand.

BLD-33.name: The Longwind line
BLD-33.trait: Long wind: runs and fights for hours like a human instead of burning out in minutes
BLD-33.how: Carriers' muscles hold about as many slow, tireless fibers as a human's, about half, instead of the orc quarter, with more fine blood vessels to feed them. They lose part of the orc burst of power but keep going for hours.
BLD-33.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of a carrier have it, from either parent.
BLD-33.cost: Weaker bursts than other orcs: in a charge they hit about as hard as a strong human. Mocked as half-human for 140 years. Runners die alone behind enemy lines.
BLD-33.exclusive: All carriers descend from Orrak the Walker, in whom the change began; no other orc line has it, and ordinary half-orcs do not have this wind.
BLD-33.ancestor: Tukar Longwind, who ran 300 km in three days to warn the clans
BLD-33.story: The first carrier was Orrak the Walker, born at Gashmar in 961. His mother was Hilde, a Northfolk farm girl taken in the Gashmar raid over the Glenwash in 954, who served seven winters as a herd-thrall and was adopted and married to the rider Varg Crow-Eye. Orrak was half human, but his wind was more than a half-orc's: his brothers by the same parents tired like any half-orc, and Orrak did not tire at all. At 12 he ran down a wounded deer over 30 km. At 15 he carried word from Gashmar to the camps on the Gnarzag, about 170 km, in a day and a night.
BLD-33.significance: In a war with Aldmark in the spring of 1105, the Longwind Runners decide whether the clans gather in time. The Horde's relays last ten minutes, but its runners last all day, and without them the war-chief is blind across 1,345,000 km² of grass.

BLD-34.name: The Oakborn
BLD-34.trait: Deep years: lives 600 years or more and ages about two-thirds as fast as other elves
BLD-34.how: A single inherited change slows the body's clock after youth. An Oakborn grows at the normal elven pace to about 50, then ages about two-thirds as fast as other elves: cells repair themselves longer, and heart, eyes and joints wear out later. The same slow clock slows fertility;
BLD-34.inherit: Behaves as a single dominant factor: about half the children of a carrier carry it, whether the other parent is elf or human. A child who does not carry it cannot pass it on. It shows by about 150, when a carrier still looks like an elf of 100.
BLD-34.cost: Very low fertility: one child in 200 years at best, and many pregnancies fail. The line has shrunk from 17 carriers to two. Long lives also mean old rulers: every Oakborn crowned since 3000 BR was over 300 at the crowning.
BLD-34.exclusive: Only children of a carrier can carry it, and only about half do. At 150 the Keepers judge each child of the line by growth and teeth;
BLD-34.ancestor: Queen Aelinwe, who planted the First Oak at Evenglade
BLD-34.story: The first known carrier was Aelinwe, born about 4390 BR among the grove-kin of Evenglade. Her age-mates grew grey and slow while she did not. At 150 she looked like an elf of 90, and the grove elders began to ask whether she was ill. She was not. At 179, when she planted the First Oak and swore the Covenant, she was a young-looking woman among elders who had nursed her. The grove-kin took it as a sign that the forest favoured her, and they made her queen. The Keepers who tended the oak counted the years from the planting partly to measure her long life.
BLD-34.significance: The Oakborn are the hinge of the Evenwood's future in 1105. If Ithrien dies without a lawful heir, the Moot's succession law is silent for the first time in 5,316 years. The Deep Root would declare the crown sleeping and rule through the Keepers;

BLD-35.name: The Mistwalkers
BLD-35.trait: True night sight: eyes that shine in lamplight and see in near-total dark
BLD-35.how: Carriers have a reflective layer behind the retina far thicker than other elves' and many more rod cells, so they see shapes by starlight under cloud where other elves see only grey. The same eyes let in too much light by day: at noon the glare blinds them, and they veil their eyes with grey gauze.
BLD-35.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of a carrier carry it. It shows in the first year, when a carrier baby's eyes shine green-gold in lamplight.
BLD-35.cost: Blinded by the noon sun: carriers veil their eyes by day and fight best at dusk. A daylight fight on open ground or an open deck finds them half-blind, as the noon raid of 611 proved.
BLD-35.exclusive: Carried only by descendants of Nimrael. At every naming a lamp is raised before the child's face; only a child whose eyes shine may ever be named Heir of the Veil, and a non-carrier child keeps the…
BLD-35.story: Nimrael was born about 200 BR at Mirlas, among the night fishers of Lake Silara. Her mother saw at once that the baby's eyes threw back the lamplight like an owl's. As a child she could see fish moving over the lake bottom by starlight and find her way through the Silara Groves on moonless nights, but at noon she wept with the glare and hid under the trees. Her mother sewed her a veil of grey nettle gauze, and she wore one all her life. The fisher-kin used her gift: she steered their boats at night and brought in catches no one else could.
BLD-35.significance: The trait holds Eldergrove's crown and its land army. Only carriers may be named heir, and the heir Ilvara commands the Night Rangers and the Dusk School. In 1105 the line matters beyond the coast.

BLD-36.name: The Quickened
BLD-36.trait: Reactions quicker than any other elf's, and far quicker than any man's
BLD-36.how: Nerve fibres carry signals faster and the brain's movement centres fire with less delay, so a carrier moves a blink sooner than another elf. The same easily fired nerves can fire out of control: flicker at a few flashes a second, such as torchlight through a crowd or lightning through leaves,…
BLD-36.inherit: About one child in three of a carrier carries it. It seems to need more than one inherited factor, so it can skip a generation and return; children of two carriers carry it about one time in two.
BLD-36.cost: Fits and seizures, often set off by flickering light such as torches, burning buildings or lightning through leaves. A fit in battle is death: Sethril died of one, and Serin was killed during one in 1079.
BLD-36.exclusive: Carried only by descendants of Sethril. The School of the Quickened tests every child of the line with the dropped rod at 30 and teaches its deepest drills only to carriers;
BLD-36.ancestor: Sethril the Unwounded, duelist unbeaten for 400 years
BLD-36.story: Sethril was born in 460 to a family of yew-cutters at Lirith. His mother noticed that he caught falling acorns before they reached the forest floor. At 40 he could pluck a thrown pebble out of the air, and the Keepers tested him with a dropped rod: he caught it a blink sooner than any elf they had ever timed. He trained under the old sword masters of Evenglade, and within a century he was the best blade in the Evenwood. In June 527 he killed the Solen knight Sir Marcus Ravel in four passes at the Oak Line, cutting his sword hand and then his throat.
BLD-36.significance: The Quickened are the queen's last line of steel. The Queen's Quickened guard Ithrien's door at Evenglade, and two of the finest blades alive, Vaelor at tier 7 and Veyla at tier 6, are carriers.

BLD-37.name: The Lightfoot
BLD-37.trait: Light bones: jumps higher and lands softer than any other people, with near-perfect balance
BLD-37.how: Carriers build thinner, lighter bones, about a fifth lighter than other elves', and their balance organs in the inner ear are unusually sharp. Less weight to lift and stop means higher jumps, softer landings and running along branches that would not hold another elf.
BLD-37.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of a carrier carry it. It shows early; a Lightfoot child walks at ten months and climbs before it talks.
BLD-37.cost: Bones break easily: a fall or a mace blow that bruises a human cripples a Lightfoot. They avoid shield walls and close melee.
BLD-37.exclusive: Carried only by descendants of Faelas Leafstep. Every child of the line is tested at ten by walking a peeled birch pole across a stream;
BLD-37.story: Faelas Leafstep was born at Rinael in 380, a small, slight child who climbed before he could talk. By 60 he could run along branches as thin as a wrist and drop 8 m from an oak to the leaf floor without a sound. He broke his arm three times before he was 100, and the Keepers who set the bones saw that they were as thin as a bird's. He became a ranger of the Eastern Edge. In August 501 a charcoal-burners' fire from the Calena woods crossed the Oak Line near Aeravel.
BLD-37.significance: The Lightfoot are the eyes and messengers of the Oak Line. Their scouts carry news across the Evenwood faster than any rider, and their captain decides whether a human logger lives or dies.

BLD-38.name: House Bardun
BLD-38.trait: Deep breath: works at 7,000 m where even dwarves gasp
BLD-38.how: Carriers make more red blood cells than other dwarves, have larger lungs and a stronger drive to breathe, and their blood takes up oxygen more readily in thin air. They can work and climb at 7,000 m.
BLD-38.inherit: About half the children of a carrier carry it. It is proved, not guessed: an heir who cannot carry the ingot to the Crown Shelf at 7,000 m does not carry it, or not strongly enough to rule.
BLD-38.cost: Suffers badly from heat and lowland air: below 1,000 m carriers sicken within weeks, and their thick blood strains the heart in old age.
BLD-38.exclusive: Carried only by descendants of Brom Bardun; dwarves cannot have fertile children with any other people, and stonebairns are sterile.
BLD-38.ancestor: King Brom Bardun, founder of Stonehold's First Hall
BLD-38.story: Brom Bardun was born about 2520 BR into a clan of prospectors on the edge of the Roof. Every dwarf of the Roof could work at 4,000 m, but Brom could climb at 6,000 m with a load and still swing a pick, and the old prospectors said he had lungs like a bellows. He spent his youth following veins of gold and tin down the southern face of the Worldspine. About 2350 BR, looking for the source of a gold vein, he climbed the great peak above the valley that became the First Hall and reached a shelf of rock at about 7,000 m where the gold-bearing quartz ran across the ice.
BLD-38.significance: The deep breath decides who holds the throne of the dwarven world's oldest realm, its Hold Bank and the seat of the Deep Law. In 1105 the trait is on trial. King Harvald is about 214 and failing;

BLD-39.name: Clan Hammerhand
BLD-39.trait: Hammer arms: upper-body strength far beyond other dwarves
BLD-39.how: In the full form the body's brake on muscle growth is weak, and the heavy muscle of the dwarven shoulders, chest and arms grows to about one and a half times its normal size and strength.
BLD-39.inherit: Recessive in full form: a child needs the factor from both parents to have hammer arms, about one child in four of two carriers. With one copy a dwarf is merely strong. The clan marries carriers, mostly cousins, to keep it.
BLD-39.cost: Enormous appetite (about 5,000 kcal a day), stiff shoulders and weak hearts: 22 carriers have died of the heart before 190.
BLD-39.exclusive: Carried only by descendants of the Hammerhand smith clan of the First Hall, and in full form only in the royal clan, which marries carrier cousins. Dwarves cannot breed with other peoples.
BLD-39.story: The Hammerhands were a smith clan of Stonehold's First Hall whose cousins had married cousins for generations, and every few generations a child was born with shoulders like a yak's. Dagna, born in 340, was the strongest of them. At twelve she could lift the horn of her father's anvil off the floor, and at 40 she could hold a 90 kg anvil above her head while the clan counted to thirty. She drew iron under the trip-hammer by hand and was a master smith at 50. Her strength made her proud, and in 398 it made her an exile.
BLD-39.significance: The hammer arms decide who rules the hold that taught Chanari, owes Ranpur 40,000 lotus and sits on a mountain that is growing hotter. In 1105 the two full carriers who can wear the crown want opposite things: Forge-Queen Hilde wants every secret kept until her escape road is done, and her heir…

BLD-40.name: Clan Deepeye
BLD-40.trait: Deep eyes: sees by the glow of a single coal
BLD-40.how: Carriers have many more rod cells in the retina than other dwarves and fewer colour cells, and their pupils open wider. They see shapes and ore seams by the glow of one coal, but bright light floods the eye and brings on crushing headaches, and they see colours poorly.
BLD-40.inherit: Dominant: about half the children of a carrier carry it. It shows in the first months, when a carrier baby cries in daylight and quiets in the dark.
BLD-40.cost: Sunlight brings on crushing headaches, and snow-glare can blind; carriers travel above ground only by night, wear hooded veils outdoors and see colours poorly.
BLD-40.exclusive: Carried only by descendants of Asa the Coal-Eyed. Dwarves cannot have fertile children with any other people, and a stonebairn is sterile, so the trait can never leave the dwarven line.
BLD-40.story: Asa was born in 480 into a clan of deep miners in one of the fourteen Iron Mountain halls. As a child she found her way through unlit galleries that other children would not enter without a lamp, and she wept and hid from the summer sun at the hall mouth. At 40 she was working the far ends of the galleries alone with one coal in a clay pot for light, reading the colour and grain of the rock where others saw only black. The miners called her the Coal-Eyed. She followed thin seams that others missed and made her small clan the richest in its hall.
BLD-40.significance: The deep eyes sit on the throne of the Westland's richest iron. In 1105 that throne is the point where Aldmark's army, Irondeep's hunger and the Deep Law meet. Brynja has secretly sold Aldmark a fort; Korrin means to set her aside at the Founding;

BLD-41.name: The Stonelungs
BLD-41.trait: Dust-proof lungs: breathe rock dust for a lifetime without the miners' cough
BLD-41.how: Their airways clear dust unusually well: thick, fast-moving mucus and many more cleaning cells in the deep lung carry rock dust out before it can scar. The same change in the lining of the nose blunts the sense of smell almost to nothing, so they cannot smell the rotten-egg or burnt smells that…
BLD-41.inherit: About half the children of a carrier carry it. It shows early as a child who cannot smell smoke or rot, and later as a miner who never coughs.
BLD-41.cost: They have almost no sense of smell and cannot smell bad air; 31 have died in gas pockets since 812.
BLD-41.exclusive: Carried only by descendants of Old Hald Stonelung. Dwarves cannot breed with other peoples, so the trait cannot leave the dwarven line.
BLD-41.story: Hald was born at Morhall in 720 into a family of tunnel-cutters, the dwarves who drive new headings through raw rock in a fog of dust. Most cutters coughed by 100 and died of the miners' cough by 150. Hald cut the dustiest headings of Morhall for a century and never coughed. His mother also noticed that as a child he could not smell bread burning. In 812 he and his work partner broke into a pocket of bad air in a new heading. The partner smelled rotten eggs and turned back too late; Hald smelled nothing, walked through it holding his breath by chance, and lived.
BLD-41.significance: The Stonelungs are the one family that sits on both sides of the quarrel between Stonehold and Emberdeep. Grimbald is Stonehold's war leader and knows Emberdeep still takes a share of Chanari's blades; Dagny has given him first dig on Emberdeep's new gold gravels without her queen's leave.

BLD-42.name: The Skarfell line
BLD-42.trait: Small giants: only 300 to 330 cm and 600 to 800 kg; they can run and turn like no other giant
BLD-42.how: A broken copy of one growth gene. In giants, as in humans, this gene works only from the copy a child gets from its father; the mother's copy is always switched off.
BLD-42.inherit: Through fathers. About half the children of a small Skarfell man are small. The children of a Skarfell woman are full-size but carry the broken copy hidden; about half of their sons' children are small again, while their daughters pass it on hidden once more.
BLD-42.cost: Weaker than other giants (about three times human strength rather than five); they feel the cold more and need heavier furs; a small Skarfell woman carrying a full-size child often dies in the birth; the line marries close and the big halls mock it as runts.
BLD-42.exclusive: Only giants can carry it, because giants cannot breed with humans. It shows only when it comes from a father, so the visible line runs through its men;
BLD-42.story: Skarvi was born at Skarfell Hall in 870 to Hogni of Skarfell, a giant of ordinary size, and Aslaug of Torvik. At a year old he was half the weight of other giant babies, and the hall thought he would die. He did not. At five he could run, which no giant child can, and at ten he could turn on his heel and climb the fair-ground fences. He grew to a small giant's height and stopped. The halls mocked him, but the tin traders took to him: he could stoop through a warehouse door, sit on a trader's bench without breaking it and stand on a ship's deck without sinking the boat.
BLD-42.significance: Frostholm holds the only large tin deposits in the western lands, and bronze for bells, mirrors, pots and fittings across the Westland depends on it. The Skarfell trait is what lets the giant halls sell that tin as one people: only a Skarfell can enter a trader's house, board a ship or sit at a…

BLD-43.name: The Jotunhall line
BLD-43.trait: Giants among giants: 430 to 460 cm and up to 1,800 kg, with immense strength
BLD-43.how: An extra copy of a growth-signal gene on the X chromosome makes the growth gland at the base of the brain overwork from early childhood, like Earth's X-linked gigantism.
BLD-43.inherit: On the X chromosome, so it runs through the Mothers. A carrier mother passes it to about half her sons, who grow to the great size, and to about half her daughters, who carry it but grow little taller than other women.
BLD-43.cost: Knees and hips fail by 40 and hearts begin to fail by 60; each of them eats 30,000 kcal and more a day, more than a household of five; they overheat sooner than other giants; a fall from their own height can kill, as it killed Hrolf in 1049.
BLD-43.exclusive: Giants cannot breed with humans, so only giants can carry it, and every carrier alive descends from Grom. The Mothers of Jotunhall arrange every marriage of the line's women at the Thing;
BLD-43.story: Grom was born at Jotunhall in 950 to Alfhild, a woman of an ordinary household, and a hunter of the hall. Nothing in either family's chant explained him. By ten he was the size of a grown giant woman; by 25 he stood a head over the tallest giant, and he kept growing until he was 30, taller than any giant in any chant. His hands could close around a walrus's skull, and he ate like three giants. The halls first took him for a sign of the Mother's favor, then for a burden, because in the hungry years his hall could hardly feed him. That changed in the Famine Winter of 991.
BLD-43.significance: The Jotunhall size is the crown of Hrimfell, and in 1105 it is the crown's problem. The Thing of Midsummer 1105 must choose between Ulfar, the only man of the size, who cannot walk to the shore, and a giant who can still fight;

REL-01.name: Temple of the Returning Sun
REL-01.followers: CUL-01 (most Solenfolk); the courts of Ashmere; about 26 million people
REL-01.belief: One Light made everything. The sun is its living face. The Devourer, a being of cold and dark, swallowed the sun at Mount Hael, and the Light returned it through Corvan, its chosen king. The sun must be honored and 'held' through its weakest night.
REL-01.afterlife: The righteous rise into the sun at the noon after their death. The wicked stay in the cold dark under Mount Hael with the Devourer. The dead are buried facing east, never burned: fire belongs to the sun.
REL-01.clergy: Priests called dawnkeepers; bishops called Luminaries; the High Luminary rules from Solenne. Priests may not marry. Orders: the Needle-Keepers (astronomer-priests who keep the calendar and the archives) and the Knights of the Sun (a military order that…
REL-01.rituals: Greeting the dawn; the noon prayer at the ringing of the noon bell; the Sunday rite; burial at dawn facing east; crowning kings on Return Day; pilgrimage to Solenne
REL-01.festivals: Lantern Night (2 February); Return Day (21 June, the greatest); Ash Night (31 October); Midwinter Vigil (21 December); Needle Day (1 January, blessing the new year's count)
REL-01.taboos: Letting a hearth fire die on Midwinter night; lying at noon; burning the dead; building on Hael's ash; working on Sunday
REL-01.politics: Rules the Holy See outright. Crowns the kings of Varenna and Morhaven and the Doge of Lucerna. Can 'unlight' (excommunicate) a ruler, freeing his subjects from their oaths.
REL-01.prophecy: The Book of Ash: 'In the year when the count of the Needle and the count of the trees agree, the Light will fail again.' Priests read it as a warning of a second Dimming.

REL-02.name: Dawn Church
REL-02.followers: CUL-11 (Eastfolk); half of Tessaria; about 11 million people
REL-02.belief: The same One Light as the Temple, but the sun is a lamp lit by the Light, not the Light itself. No bishop rules all others; each church is led by its own patriarch.
REL-02.afterlife: The righteous go to the Morning Country beyond the sunrise; the wicked wander in the night. The dead are buried facing east.
REL-02.clergy: Married priests; celibate monks; the Patriarch of Dawn at Velgrad, with lesser patriarchs at Drevna and Tessar.
REL-02.rituals: Services in the Eastfolk tongue, not Old Solen; the Dawn Liturgy at sunrise; pilgrimage to watch Redcrown's glow
REL-02.festivals: Dawn Feast (20 March, the spring equinox, the greatest); Return Day (21 June); Midwinter Vigil (21 December)
REL-02.taboos: Praying facing west; a priest serving unmarried; eating meat on the fast days of Lent-like 'Dark Weeks' (the four weeks before the spring equinox)
REL-02.politics: The Patriarch crowns the kings of Velgrad and Drevna. The Church backs one of the two claimants in the Tessarian civil war.
REL-02.prophecy: 'The Lamp will be lit anew in the East when the old sun-city falls.' Dawn churchmen read it as the fall of Solenne.

REL-03.name: The Seven Halls
REL-03.followers: CUL-02 (Northfolk); the common people of Ashmere; about 21 million people
REL-03.belief: Seven gods, each keeping a hall: the Oathfather (law, kings, oaths), the Hearth Mother (home, birth), the Smith, the Hunter, the Plough-Wife (harvest), the Sea King, and the Grey Ferryman (death).
REL-03.afterlife: Oath-keepers and the brave go to the Oathfather's hall; ordinary folk to the Grey Ferryman's quiet shore; oath-breakers are drowned forever in the Sea King's cold deep. Northreach burns its great dead in ships; Aldmark buries them in mounds.
REL-03.clergy: Hall-priests, who may marry and are often hereditary; the High Hall-Keeper at Kingsmere, appointed by the Emperor of Aldmark since the Iron Reform.
REL-03.rituals: Oaths sworn on an iron ring; animal sacrifice at the great feasts; feasting in the halls; mound and ship burials
REL-03.festivals: Oathfather's Day (1 January, oaths renewed); the Plough-Wife's Day (1 May); the Hunter's Feast (11 November, the Slaughter Feast); the Long Night of the Halls (21 December)
REL-03.taboos: Breaking an oath sworn on iron (the breaker is outlawed); harming a guest; eating horse, which is sacred to the Hunter
REL-03.politics: In Aldmark the Emperor is the faith's head and priests judge oath cases. Elsewhere halls are local and weak at the top.
REL-03.prophecy: 'Three winters without a summer will end the world, and the halls will burn.' Scholars think it is a memory of the Dimming. The prophecy of the Iron House, 'An Ironside will fall into the water and the empire with him', is repeated in whispers.

REL-04.name: The Green Covenant
REL-04.followers: CUL-19 and CUL-20 (all elves); many half-elves; about 1.2 million people
REL-04.belief: The forest is one living whole, and the elves made a covenant with it: take only what grows back, and it will shelter them. There are no gods. Every elf's life returns into a tree at death.
REL-04.afterlife: The dead are buried under a sapling; their life passes into the tree, and a child born near it may carry something of them.
REL-04.clergy: Grove Keepers, who mark the trees and approve every cutting; the Eldest Keeper tends the First Oak at Evenglade.
REL-04.rituals: Tree-burial; naming a child under its birth tree; the Keepers' marking of trees to be cut; asking a tree's pardon before felling
REL-04.festivals: The Greening (20 March); Leaf Fall (22 September); the Silent Night (21 June, midsummer, when no lamps are lit in the forest)
REL-04.taboos: Cutting a living tree without a Keeper's mark; open fire in the deep forest; burying the dead in stone
REL-04.politics: Keepers sit in the Moot of Leaves and can veto any cutting; no Sylvaran law may harm the forest.
REL-04.prophecy: 'When the last Oakborn dies, the forest will burn.' The Oakborn line is close to dying out.

REL-05.name: The Deep Law
REL-05.belief: The Smith-Father forged the world on the anvil of the deep fire. The ancestors watch from their halls under the mountain. The Law was carved in the First Hall by King Brom Bardun and must be kept.
REL-05.afterlife: The dead are laid in rock vaults and join the Ancestors' Hall deep in the mountain. The unburied wander in the cold.
REL-05.clergy: Law-Carvers, who keep the carved law and the genealogies and serve as judges; the Eldest Carver sits in the First Hall of Stonehold.
REL-05.rituals: Oaths sealed by pouring molten metal into a mold marked with both names; the name-carving at age 30; burial in rock
REL-05.festivals: The Kindling (21 December: every forge is put out and relit from the First Hall's fire); the Founding (the anniversary of the First Hall, 3 March)
REL-05.taboos: Revealing a forge secret; breaking a contract; leaving a dwarf unburied under open sky
REL-05.politics: Law-Carvers are the holds' judges; no king may change carved law without the Carvers.
REL-05.prophecy: 'The mountain will open and the old fire will return.' Dwarves fear it means an eruption under Emberdeep, whose hot springs have grown hotter in the last 50 years.

REL-06.name: The Way of the Open Sky
REL-06.followers: CUL-12 (Skyfolk); pilgrims from Ranpur and the Free Marches; about 400,000 people
REL-06.belief: All life turns through rebirth. The high, clear air is closer to the clarity that ends the turning. Kindness and stillness lead upward; cruelty and craving lead down.
REL-06.afterlife: Rebirth according to one's deeds, until a soul is clear enough to pass into the Open Sky and turn no more. The dead are given to the vultures and bone-breakers on high platforms: sky burial.
REL-06.clergy: Monks and nuns (most families give one child); abbots of the monasteries; the Abbot of the White Stair at Skyhold, found as a child who is believed to be the reborn previous abbot. The present abbot is the 13th.
REL-06.rituals: Prayer flags and prayer wheels; butter lamps; walking the circuit of Lake Bluespire; sky burial
REL-06.festivals: The Sky New Year (the new moon nearest 15 February, by their own moon calendar); the Bluespire Circuit season (June to August); Lamp Night (the full moon of October)
REL-06.taboos: Killing any animal on monastery land; burning the dead; climbing the sacred peaks
REL-06.politics: Rules Skyhold outright; the Abbot is head of state.
REL-06.prophecy: 'When the Fourteenth dies, the White Stair will crack.' The 13th Abbot is 53 and ailing.

REL-07.name: The Path of the Well
REL-07.followers: CUL-04, CUL-05, CUL-07 (Qadiri, Sandfolk, Sabrans); the Amber sultans; many Zanari merchants; two tribes of the Nine Winds;
REL-07.belief: One God, the Giver of Water, who made the world and sends rain. The prophet Samar the Water-Finder (about 512–581 AR) found water in the Red Waste and spoke the sayings gathered in the Book of Wells.
REL-07.afterlife: The righteous drink forever in the Garden of Springs; the wicked thirst.
REL-07.clergy: No priests. Well-Keepers are scholars and judges of the Book of Wells; the Keeper of the First Well guards the Well of Samar with the Sand Clans.
REL-07.rituals: Prayer at dawn, noon and dusk after washing the hands; the water-alms: every household must give water to any traveler; the Dry Month of fasting
REL-07.festivals: Well Day (14 March, when Samar found water); the Dry Month (all of August, fasting from dawn to dusk); the Breaking of the Dry (1 September)
REL-07.taboos: Fouling water; refusing water to a traveler; making images of the Giver; drunkenness; blood feud within sight of a well
REL-07.politics: Well-Keepers judge the law in Qadir, Sabra and the Amber Isles; sultans call themselves Guardians of the Water.
REL-07.prophecy: 'The Well-Finder will return when the last well runs dry.'

REL-08.name: The Flood Mother
REL-08.belief: The Flood Mother is the Monuti River. Her husband the Sun-Boat sails the sky by day and the Night River by night. The King of Tamar is her son, a living god, and the flood comes because he is.
REL-08.afterlife: The dead sail west on the Night River and need their bodies in the next life, so bodies are dried in natron from the Burning Waste and wrapped.
REL-08.clergy: Flood-priests, who measure the river on the Flood Stairs at Tamar and set each year's tax from the flood height; the High Flood-Priest.
REL-08.rituals: Offerings to the rising water; preserving the dead in natron; the king's yearly 'cutting of the dykes'
REL-08.festivals: The Tears (15 August, the flood's first rise); the Opening of the Dykes (1 September); the Harvest of the Mother (1 March)
REL-08.taboos: Killing an ibis; fishing on flood-days; killing the crocodiles during the flood
REL-08.politics: The king is divine; the flood-priests hold the tax records and can declare a bad flood a sign that the Mother has turned away from him.
REL-08.prophecy: 'When the river fails three years, the Mother abandons her son.' A three-year failure would undo the king's right to rule.

REL-09.name: The Thousand Ancestors
REL-09.followers: CUL-08, CUL-09, CUL-10 (Zanari, Abari, Keshi); the Western Veld; about 19 million people
REL-09.belief: The High One made the world and withdrew. The ancestors remain near and speak for the living as long as they are remembered. The emperor of Zanara is the chief voice of all ancestors.
REL-09.afterlife: The dead become ancestors who stay close while their names are spoken; the forgotten dead fade into nothing. Many are buried under the house floor.
REL-09.clergy: Rememberers, who keep the genealogies and songs; mask societies who dance the ancestors; the High Rememberer at the Ancestor Hill of Zanara.
REL-09.rituals: Libations to the ancestors; mask dances; reciting genealogies at every naming, wedding and funeral
REL-09.festivals: The Night of Masks (1 October, end of the rains); First Millet (15 September); the Emperor's Remembering (on each dead emperor's day)
REL-09.taboos: Speaking the name of a dead king aloud outside a rite; eating one's clan animal
REL-09.politics: The emperor's right to rule comes from his ancestors; Rememberers can refuse to sing a king's line, which is a crisis.
REL-09.prophecy: 'The Runner who never tires will carry the empire across the sand.' The Kanemba line claims it.

REL-10.name: The Thousand Names
REL-10.followers: CUL-13 (Ranpuri); commoners of the Amber Isles; about 8 million people
REL-10.belief: One divine with a thousand faces: gods of the monsoon, the river, the elephant, the forge, death, and many more. Souls are reborn according to their deeds.
REL-10.afterlife: Rebirth; the dead are burned on river banks and their ashes given to the river.
REL-10.clergy: Temple families who serve hereditary shrines; the High Priest of the Great Temple of Ranpur.
REL-10.rituals: Offerings of flowers and lamps; bathing in rivers; processions with elephants; cremation
REL-10.festivals: Monsoon Welcome (15 June); the Festival of Lamps (25 October); the Elephant Day (1 February)
REL-10.taboos: Harming the white elephant; killing any elephant without the king's leave; eating the flesh of the sacred river fish
REL-10.politics: Temples own land and hold their own courts; the king is their patron and protector.
REL-10.prophecy: 'When the white elephant dies without a calf, the dream will end.' The white elephant Moon-Pearl is 58 and has no calf.

REL-11.name: The Storm and the Mare
REL-11.followers: CUL-22, CUL-23 (all orcs); many half-orcs; some Wind Riders; about 2.5 million people
REL-11.belief: The Storm-Father (sky and thunder) and the Mare-Mother (earth and grass) made the world. The ancestors ride the storm. Shamans drum to speak with them.
REL-11.afterlife: The dead ride with the storm across the Grass Beyond. They are laid on high platforms on hilltops; great chiefs are buried with their horses.
REL-11.clergy: Shamans (drummers), trained for years; the Grey Mothers keep the spoken law; in the Horde a Drum Council of senior shamans.
REL-11.rituals: Horse sacrifice at great funerals; libations of mare's milk; drumming and sweat lodges; the Law of the Fire (hospitality)
REL-11.festivals: Storm Coming (the first thunder of spring, movable); the Great Ride (21 June: races and clan councils at the Drum Stones); the Winter Count (the first snow, when each clan paints its winter picture)
REL-11.taboos: Spilling mare's milk carelessly; harming a guest; refusing food to a guest; killing a shaman
REL-11.politics: Shamans confirm war-chiefs; the Grey Mothers can overrule them on matters of law.
REL-11.prophecy: 'A rider born of two peoples will unite all the grass.' Half-orcs across the steppe are watched for signs of it.

REL-12.name: The Mother Under the Ice
REL-12.followers: CUL-24 (giants); the human tribute-folk of Frostholm and Hrimfell
REL-12.belief: A great mother sleeps under the ice and sends seals and whales to her children. Each whale carries an ancestor's soul.
REL-12.afterlife: The dead go down under the ice to the Mother.
REL-12.clergy: None; the eldest of each hall leads rites.
REL-12.rituals: Lineage chants; thanking the whale; giving the dead to the sea
REL-12.festivals: The Thing (every seven years at each giant land: Hrimfell's next at Midsummer 1105
REL-12.taboos: Frostholm's at the Thingvold in 1106 AR)

REL-13.name: The Drowned Queen
REL-13.followers: Sailors and fisherfolk of every coast
REL-13.belief: A queen who drowned in the first storm rules the sea; sailors give her coins and wine before a voyage.
REL-13.afterlife: The drowned serve in her hall.
REL-13.rituals: Pouring wine over the bow; throwing a coin at Sea Opening
REL-13.festivals: Sea Opening (1 April); Sea Closing (1 October)
REL-13.taboos: Whistling on deck; women on some ships (not on Corsair ships)

REL-14.name: The Eternal Blue
REL-14.belief: The endless sky is the highest power; spirits live in springs, hills and the Salt Sea.
REL-14.afterlife: The dead ride into the sky on the smoke of their funeral fire.
REL-14.rituals: Tying blue cloth to cairns; libations of milk to the sky
REL-14.taboos: Washing in running water in spring; stepping on a threshold

REL-15.name: The Ashen
REL-15.followers: A few thousand in Ashmere, Varenna and the Holy See
REL-15.belief: Mount Hael is a god that ate the sun and could eat it again. It must be fed with offerings, or it will wake. Some members want it to wake and end the world.
REL-15.afterlife: The faithful will be spared when the mountain wakes.
REL-15.rituals: Offerings of ash and blood; rubbing ash on the eyelids
REL-15.festivals: Ash Night (31 October), turned to their own use
REL-15.politics: Hunted as heretics by the Temple; a member caught is burned in effigy and imprisoned for life.
REL-15.prophecy: 'The mountain will speak again in the year of the two counts.' They read the Temple's own prophecy as theirs.

REL-16.name: The Forest Spirits
REL-16.belief: Every tree, river and animal has a spirit; hunters ask pardon of their prey.
REL-16.rituals: Songs before a hunt; honey offerings

REL-17.name: The Marchland Saints
REL-17.belief: A mix of every faith brought by settlers, around local saints who were once real people: healers, bandit-slayers and founders of free towns.
REL-17.afterlife: Whatever each settler's home faith says.
REL-17.rituals: Pilgrimage to saints' graves; oaths on a saint's bones
REL-17.politics: Saints' shrines are neutral ground for Marchland meetings.

REL-18.name: The Hearth Folk
REL-18.followers: Country people across the Westland, alongside their main faith
REL-18.belief: Small house-spirits guard every hearth, barn and well, and must be left milk and bread.
REL-18.rituals: A saucer of milk by the hearth at night
REL-18.taboos: Insulting the house-spirit; moving house without asking it

REL-19.name: Luck-gods of the Corsairs
REL-19.belief: A crowd of luck-gods borrowed from every coast: the Drowned Queen, the Grey Ferryman, a laughing god of dice.
REL-19.afterlife: The brave dead drink in the Drowned Queen's hall.
REL-19.taboos: Harming a crew-mate at sea; breaking a share-out

wars: Solen city-states; Corvan of Solenne wins; crowned 1 AR.
Solen Kingdom vs the free cities of the western Sunlands; Solen wins.
Solen vs orc clans raiding through the Crown Range passes; draw, border at the Crown Range.
Solen conquers the Long Rift; Tamar becomes a province.
Solen vs Sylvaran; elves win; Treaty of the Oak Line (302).
Solen vs the Crown highland clans; Charter of Highcastle (336) grants self-rule: the Highland League.
Solen conquers the Free Marches and the Neck.
Solen vs Wind Rider tribes of the Salt Steppe; Solen wins the shore, fails inland.
Solen vs the Old Horde (HPOL-07); Old Horde destroyed; the Crown Wall built (474–489).
Samar's heirs vs Solen governors; Qadir independent (604).
Stonehold vs Solen governors of the Neck over Zardeep Pass tolls; Stonehold wins the right to tolls.
three claimants after Justinian IV; Emperor Valerian II wins; empire weakened.
the grandsons of Valerian II fight over the throne; the empire loses its last Southland footholds, Rashira and Kadah; Emperor Theodoric I wins in 668.
the Neck breaks from Solen; Kingdom of Tessaria.
Varenna breaks away after the Dawn Schism.
mutinous generals and Varennan and Morhaven armies besiege Solenne; last emperor Constantine IX killed 759; the Holy See takes over (760).
Ulagan conquers the Grass Sea, the orc clans and the Free Marches.
the Wind Empire fails to take Morhaven.
Mosi the Runner unites the Golden Plains.
Tessaria takes the Free Marches and the Long Rift.
Harald Ironside unites the northern plains.

Greyhaven vs Velgrad over channel tolls; Treaty of the Two Shores (1010) splits tolls.
over the Palella trade; Varenna wins trade rights.
Gorath the Great unites the orc clans; Battle of the Salt Shore (1041) defeats the Nine Winds.
the Tessarian Empire collapses; Anselm Six-Fingers keeps only the Neck, as King of Tessaria.
Aldmark vs the Horde; ends in the Peace of the Glenwash (1052), a border on the Glenwash's tributary Gordush.
twin heirs of Abara fight; ends in a split crown shared in alternate years.
Lucerna and Varenna vs Blackreef; Blackreef survives; "dragon tolls" begin.
Zanara vs the Sand Clans over the salt-gold trade.

Grakka Ironhide unites the Tusk Clans and fights Drevna.
Horde vs Aldmark; Horde takes the upper Gordush.

Ranpur vs Stonehold over the Nagora Pass.
Northreach and the Free Halls resist Aldmark's claim over their faith; a Greyhaven squadron blockades Wolfhaven for Aldmark (1092); Aldmark backs down.
